## Proposition 13.1
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the greater segment added to the half of the whole is five times the square on the half.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, AC being the greater segment. Bisect AB at E [1.10], so that AE = EB. Produce BA beyond A [P2], and on the produced part cut off AD equal to AE [1.3]. Then AD = AE = EB, so AD is the half of the whole AB. The points D, A, C, B lie in this order on one straight line; hence DC is a straight line cut at A into the segments DA, AC, and AB is a straight line cut at E into the equal segments AE, EB. We must show that the square on DC (the greater segment AC together with the half AD) is five times the square on AD.

**Step 2.** Since AB is cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, AC being the greater segment, by D6.3, as AB is to AC, so is AC to CB.

**Step 3.** Thus the three straight lines AB, AC, CB are proportional, so by 6.17 the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the square on the mean: rect(AB, CB) = sq(AC).

**Step 4.** Since AB is cut at C, by 2.2 the rectangles contained by the whole and each segment together equal the square on the whole: rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB) = sq(AB). By Step 3, rect(AB, CB) = sq(AC); adding rect(AB, AC) to these equals [CN2], rect(AB, AC) + sq(AC) = rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB), and therefore [CN1] rect(AB, AC) + sq(AC) = sq(AB).

**Step 5.** Since DC is cut at A, by 2.4 the square on the whole equals the squares on the segments together with twice the rectangle contained by the segments: sq(DC) = sq(DA) + sq(AC) + 2 rect(DA, AC).

**Step 6.** Since AB is cut at E into AE, EB, by 2.1 the rectangle contained by AC and AB equals the rectangles contained by AC and each segment: rect(AC, AB) = rect(AC, AE) + rect(AC, EB). By D2.1 a rectangle is contained, and so determined, by the two straight lines about its right angle; since AE and EB are each equal to AD, rect(AC, AE) = rect(AC, AD) and rect(AC, EB) = rect(AC, AD). Hence [CN2, CN1] rect(AB, AC) = 2 rect(DA, AC).

**Step 7.** Since AB is cut at E, by 2.4 sq(AB) = sq(AE) + sq(EB) + 2 rect(AE, EB). Because AE = EB, the rectangle contained by AE, EB is equilateral as well as right-angled, that is, it is the square on AE [D1.22]; and because AE and EB are each equal to AD, the squares on AE and on EB are each equal to the square on AD. Therefore [CN2] sq(AB) = sq(AD) + sq(AD) + 2 sq(AD) = 4 sq(AD).

**Step 8.** Combining these results: sq(DC) = sq(AD) + sq(AC) + 2 rect(DA, AC) [Step 5] = sq(AD) + sq(AC) + rect(AB, AC) [Step 6, CN2] = sq(AD) + sq(AB) [Step 4, CN2] = sq(AD) + 4 sq(AD) [Step 7, CN2] = 5 sq(AD).

**Step 9.** Therefore the square on DC, which is the greater segment AC added to the half AD of the whole, is five times the square on the half AD. This is what was to be proved.

Path note: the identity sq(DC) = sq(AB) + sq(AD) was obtained directly from the Book II area propositions (2.1, 2.2, 2.4) rather than by describing squares and comparing gnomons; the Book II route is the more direct.

heath_proof_text: For let the straight line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio at the point C, and let AC be the greater segment; let the straight line AD be produced in a straight line with CA, and let AD be made half of AB; I say that the square on CD is five times the square on AD. For let the squares AE, DF be described on AB, DC, and let the figure in DF be drawn; let FC be carried through to G. Now, since AB has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, therefore the rectangle AB, BC is equal to the square on AC. [VI. Def. 3, VI. 17] And CE is the rectangle AB, BC, and FH the square on AC; therefore CE is equal to FH. And, since BA is double of AD, while BA is equal to KA, and AD to AH, therefore KA is also double of AH. But, as KA is to AH, so is CK to CH; [VI. 1] therefore CK is double of CH. But LH, HC are also double of CH. Therefore KC is equal to LH, HC. But CE was also proved equal to HF; therefore the whole square AE is equal to the gnomon MNO. And, since BA is double of AD, the square on BA is quadruple of the square on AD, that is, AE is quadruple of DH. But AE is equal to the gnomon MNO; therefore the gnomon MNO is also quadruple of AP; therefore the whole DF is five times AP. And DF is the square on DC, and AP the square on DA; therefore the square on CD is five times the square on DA.
